Floating-point addition is not associative because modern hardware represents real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, changing the grouping of additions does not change the result: adding a, b, and c as (a + b) + c is equivalent to a + (b + c). In floating-point arithmetic, however, each intermediate result is usually rounded to the nearest representable value. Since the two groupings produce different intermediate values, they may undergo different rounding and yield different final answers.

The effect is especially visible when numbers have very different magnitudes. If a very small number is added to a very large number, the small contribution may lie below the available precision and disappear during rounding. If several small numbers are added together first, their combined value may become large enough to affect the later addition. Cancellation also matters: subtracting nearly equal values can discard many significant digits, making subsequent rounding errors relatively important. IEEE 754 arithmetic specifies formats and rounding behavior, but it does not make addition associative. Features such as fused multiply-add can further change results because they compute a multiplication and addition with only one final rounding instead of rounding each operation separately.

Large matrix multiplications contain many dot products. Each output element is formed by summing products of corresponding row and column entries. Mathematically, the products may be reduced in any order. On modern CPUs and GPUs, performance depends on parallel execution, vector instructions, cache tiling, and tree-shaped reductions. Different thread counts, block sizes, scheduling decisions, libraries, or hardware architectures can therefore combine partial sums in different orders. Even when every individual operation follows IEEE 754 rules, altered reduction orders can produce slightly different output values.

These differences are usually small, often a few units in the last place, but they can grow when dot products are long, data are poorly scaled, or severe cancellation occurs. Small discrepancies may also be amplified by later computations, especially in iterative algorithms, threshold comparisons, or numerically unstable procedures. Consequently, two mathematically equivalent matrix multiplications may not be bit-for-bit reproducible across runs or platforms.

Reproducibility requires controlling more than the input and formula. Implementations may need deterministic scheduling and a fixed reduction tree, while disabling optimizations that alter operation order or contraction. More robust approaches include higher-precision accumulation, compensated or pairwise summation, and specialized reproducible accumulators. These methods can improve consistency and accuracy, but they commonly reduce performance or require additional storage and computation.
